title: The Normal Curve and z-Scores
summary: A normal density is drawn on fixed score and density axes, so that moving the mean slides the curve and raising the standard deviation visibly flattens it - the peak height is printed beside the picture and halves when the standard deviation doubles. The learner places a raw score, reads its z, its percentile and both tail areas, and highlights the one, two and three standard-deviation regions to find that their areas never move however far the two parameters are dragged. A second experiment puts the same raw mark on two different distributions and withholds both z-scores until a judgement has been committed.
learningObjectives: State what the mean and the standard deviation each do to a normal curve.
Compute a z-score and read the percentile and tail areas that go with it.
Distinguish a z-score, a percentile, a one-tailed area and a two-tailed area.
Explain why the same raw score can be ordinary in one distribution and remarkable in another.
Explain why the 68-95-99.7 figures are properties of the normal model rather than of data.
interactionTypes: live density curve with shaded area
two-distribution comparison with the answer withheld
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every value is computed in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, selects, radio groups, checkboxes and buttons, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend; the raw-score slider announces both the score and the z it produces. Both charts are hidden from assistive technology and paired inside their figures with visible tables - raw score, z, area below and area above for the single curve, and a five-column row per test for the comparison - and a disclosure lists landmark z-scores against the raw scores they correspond to on the current distribution. The shaded region below the score carries a vertical hatch as well as a fill, the score is a labelled rule, the mean is a dashed rule, and the second curve is dashed and named at its own peak, so nothing depends on colour. Percentages below 0.05 per cent are printed as such rather than rounded to zero. Pinned primary results measure 517px and 375px tall at 1366x768. Every slider, highlight and reveal announces a full sentence through the polite live region, focus moves to each experiment's heading as it opens, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths with no horizontal page scroll.
readmeTopic: Two numbers make the whole curve, and a raw score means nothing without them
simulationNotes: No data are generated at all in Experiment 1: the curve is the mathematical normal density, drawn on a score axis fixed at 0 to 100 and a density axis fixed at 0 to 0.21, which is a little above the tallest peak the sliders allow. Fixing both axes is the design decision that makes the demonstration work, because it lets the peak visibly fall as the standard deviation rises and makes the constant total area credible rather than merely asserted. Areas come from the standard normal cumulative function using the Abramowitz and Stegun 26.2.17 rational approximation, whose absolute error is below 1.5e-7 - ample for a percentile printed to one decimal place. The highlighted standard-deviation region has area twice Phi(k) minus one, which is why it never changes when the mean or standard deviation move. Experiment 2 withholds both z-scores until the learner commits to a judgement, and changing any setting after a reveal hides them again; this is a deliberate and documented exception to showing every consequence live, since the primary picture stays on screen throughout and only the two numbers that answer the question are held back. Set me a new pair draws a fresh mean, standard deviation and shared mark from a seeded generator. All tests, marks and students are fictional, and no number on the page is a norm, a benchmark or a cut-off.
